COLDWAR_SOV_gre_the_garrison_party: Marshal Andrei Grechko has run the Ministry of Defence since 1967, and in his hands the party itself begins to resemble a garrison. Officers sit beside obkom secretaries, military-patriotic education reaches every school and factory, and the defence of the motherland becomes the measure of every policy. Critics whisper of a state run from Arbat Square, but the Marshal answers that a besieged camp must be commanded, not debated.
COLDWAR_SOV_ust_the_armourer: Dmitry Ustinov became People's Commissar of Armaments in June 1941, at just thirty-two, and has managed Soviet weapons production ever since. Now the man who armed the Red Army against Hitler leads the party itself. His course is plain: the defence industry is the backbone of the state, and everything else, from the plan to the consumer, must learn to live alongside it.
COLDWAR_SOV_ust_the_military_industrial_: Leonid Smirnov has chaired the Military-Industrial Commission of the Council of Ministers since 1963, quietly coordinating ministries, design bureaus and factories across the Union. Under a General Secretary who built this system himself, the commission gains new weight. Its decisions now bind Gosplan as well as the defence ministries, and new armaments plants rise wherever it points on the map.
COLDWAR_SOV_ust_the_design_bureaus: The names of Tupolev, Sukhoi, Mikoyan, Chelomei and Yangel carry more prestige than those of most ministers. Their design bureaus compete fiercely for state orders, test sites and talent, and every new prototype is a matter of national pride. By granting them new experimental facilities and shielding them from the worst of the bureaucracy, the leadership hopes to keep Soviet engineering a generation ahead of the West.
COLDWAR_SOV_ust_the_nine_ministries: Nine all-Union ministries, from Medium Machine Building to Aviation, Shipbuilding and the Radio Industry, form the industrial heart of Soviet defence. Insiders simply call them the Nine, and their true budgets are among the best-kept secrets of the state. Binding them more tightly together promises cheaper weapons and shorter supply chains, at the price of an ever larger and more privileged apparatus.
COLDWAR_SOV_ust_quality_or_quantity: The Soviet armed forces have always relied on numbers, but the West is pulling ahead in electronics, precision and engines. The Armourer must decide where the defence industry's resources go next. One path pours money into cutting-edge research and expensive new systems, while the other keeps the assembly lines of Nizhny Tagil and Kharkov running at full speed in the belief that mass will tell in the end.
COLDWAR_SOV_ust_quality: A single modern weapon, the argument goes, is worth a dozen obsolete ones. Research institutes receive priority funding, tolerances are tightened and new designs are pushed into service even when they cost far more per unit. The army will field less hardware than its planners might wish, but every tank, aircraft and missile it does field should match or surpass its NATO counterpart.
COLDWAR_SOV_ust_the_fourth_generation: American F-15s and F-16s are entering service, and the Soviet air forces need an answer. The Mikoyan and Sukhoi bureaus are tasked with a new generation of light and heavy fighters, built around powerful turbofans, pulse-Doppler radar and exceptional agility. The future MiG-29 and Su-27 will be costly and difficult to build, but they are meant to win back the skies over Central Europe.
COLDWAR_SOV_ust_t80_and_the_gas_turbine: Ustinov has long championed a tank driven by a gas turbine rather than a diesel. The result, developed in Leningrad and adopted in 1976 as the T-80, is fast, powerful and thirsty, and far more expensive than the T-72 rolling off the lines in the Urals. Backing it fully means accepting that cost for the sake of a spearhead able to race across the North German Plain.
COLDWAR_SOV_ust_quantity: Wars, the Marshal's generation learned in 1941, are won by the side that can still deliver tanks when the first battles are over. New armaments plants are built, proven designs are kept in production instead of being replaced and unit costs are driven down relentlessly. The Soviet Army will field more divisions, more guns and more armour than any opponent can hope to destroy.
COLDWAR_SOV_ust_standardise_the_arsenal: Dozens of overlapping designs strain both the supply system and the factories. By standardising calibres, engines, chassis and components across the services, planners hope to cut costs, simplify training and keep production lines running smoothly when one model gives way to the next. It is the unglamorous side of armament, but the generals of 1941 remember well what chaos in the arsenal can cost.
COLDWAR_SOV_ust_the_stockpiles: Across Russia and the Urals lie vast hidden depots of fuel, ammunition, spare parts and mothballed equipment, held by the State Reserve for the day of mobilisation. Expanding them ties up resources the civilian economy badly needs, but ensures that a Soviet Army cut off from its factories could still fight for months. In a long war, what has already been stored may decide the outcome.
COLDWAR_SOV_ust_the_rocket_men: Valentin Glushko, Vladimir Chelomei and Vladimir Utkin lead the great rocket design bureaus, and their rivalries are as legendary as their engines. Each wants priority for his own missiles and launchers, from heavy silo-based ICBMs to the Proton. Ustinov knows all of them personally and intends to harness their competition, giving the Strategic Rocket Forces and the space programme the very best they can build.
COLDWAR_SOV_ust_ss20_deployment: The new RSD-10 Pioneer, known in the West as the SS-20, is a mobile intermediate-range missile with three warheads, able to strike any target in Western Europe within minutes. Deploying it in numbers would modernise the Soviet theatre arsenal at a stroke. It would also alarm Bonn and the other NATO capitals, and may well provoke the Americans into stationing new missiles of their own on European soil.
COLDWAR_SOV_ust_energia_buran: The American Space Shuttle programme has convinced the military that the United States intends to dominate orbit. Ustinov backs a Soviet answer on a grand scale: the super-heavy Energia rocket and the reusable Buran orbiter, developed under Glushko at NPO Energia. The project will swallow billions of rubles and years of effort, but it promises to keep Soviet spaceflight equal to anything launched from Cape Canaveral.
COLDWAR_SOV_ust_the_closed_cities: Arzamas-16, Chelyabinsk-65 and Krasnoyarsk-26 appear on no public map. In these closed cities, scientists and engineers live behind fences and checkpoints, better supplied than most Soviet citizens, and work on nuclear weapons and the materials to build them. Expanding this secret archipelago brings new laboratories and reactors into being and keeps the country's best minds devoted to the needs of defence.
COLDWAR_SOV_ust_dual_use_lines: The defence ministries already turn out refrigerators, televisions and washing machines alongside missiles and tanks, and for most Soviet consumers these goods are the only face of the military-industrial complex they will ever see. Formalising such dual-use lines brings new civilian capacity to the armaments plants. Quality remains uneven and the military always comes first, but households from Minsk to Vladivostok will notice the difference.
COLDWAR_SOV_ust_the_foreign_line: Since the April Revolution of 1978, the communist government in Kabul has torn itself apart while rebellion spreads across the Afghan countryside. Its leaders beg Moscow for help, and the Politburo must decide how far to go. Some argue that only Soviet troops can save the revolution, while others warn that the army would be walking into a war no outside power has ever won.
COLDWAR_SOV_ust_the_hawk: In December 1979, Ustinov stood alongside Andropov and Gromyko in pressing for intervention, and now the decision is his alone. The 40th Army crosses the Amu Darya to secure Kabul and the main cities, while the General Staff promises a short campaign. The officers who return will be battle-hardened, but the West sees only Soviet aggression, and the mountains will not be pacified quickly.
COLDWAR_SOV_ust_arms_not_soldiers: Instead of sending Soviet divisions into Afghanistan, Moscow sends weapons, advisers and money. The government in Kabul must fight its own war, backed by Soviet helicopters and armour but not by Soviet conscripts. The same approach is extended to friendly regimes from Angola to Ethiopia and Syria, turning the output of the defence industry into influence and hard currency without the risk of a quagmire.
COLDWAR_SOV_ust_the_heir: Ustinov is in his seventies, and even the man who built the Soviet arsenal cannot outrun time. Before he goes, he must decide who will inherit not only the party but also the defence complex he has shaped for four decades. The candidates represent two very different futures: the disciplined technocracy of Leningrad, or the energetic new generation from Stavropol.
COLDWAR_SOV_ust_heir_romanov: Grigory Romanov, the hard-driving first secretary of Leningrad, shares the Armourer's faith in industrial discipline and military strength. His city builds tanks, warships and electronics, and he has never shown the slightest sympathy for reformist experiments. By naming him successor, Ustinov ensures that the defence complex keeps its privileged place and that the course set in the Kremlin continues unbroken.
COLDWAR_SOV_ust_heir_gorbachev: Mikhail Gorbachev, the young agriculture secretary from Stavropol, is energetic, educated and popular with the reform-minded members of the Politburo. Choosing him is a gamble for the old Marshal, since Gorbachev talks of efficiency and modernisation rather than more tanks. Yet Ustinov may conclude that only a younger man can keep the economy strong enough to carry the weight of Soviet defence.
COLDWAR_SOV_ust_the_arsenal_of_socialism: Under Ustinov, the Soviet Union becomes the arsenal of world socialism. Factories from the Urals to the Volga turn out weapons for the Warsaw Pact and for allies on three continents, design bureaus race to field ever better systems and the whole economy bends to the needs of defence. Whether the people can carry this burden indefinitely is a question for another day.
COLDWAR_SOV_gro_the_leningrad_order: Grigory Romanov has ruled Leningrad since 1970 with an iron grip and a manager's eye for numbers. Now he brings the Leningrad model to the whole Union: strict discipline in the party, close ties between science and industry and zero tolerance for ideological deviation. The order that made the city on the Neva a showcase of efficiency is to be applied from Kaliningrad to Kamchatka.
COLDWAR_SOV_gro_the_leningrad_cadres: Every General Secretary brings his own people to Moscow, and Romanov is no exception. Trusted secretaries and managers from the Leningrad obkom move into key departments of the Central Committee and the ministries, displacing the old networks of the Brezhnev era. The newcomers are capable and loyal, but the established nomenklatura resents losing its comfortable positions to the men from the north.
COLDWAR_SOV_gro_the_kirov_works: The Kirov Works, LOMO and the Admiralty Shipyards form Leningrad's belt of heavy and defence industry, building tanks, optics and warships. Romanov knows these plants intimately and considers them the pride of the Soviet working class. Expanding their capacity and channelling new orders their way strengthens the defence complex and binds its managers closely to the new General Secretary.
COLDWAR_SOV_gro_science_production_assoc: Leningrad pioneered the science-production association, merging research institutes, design bureaus and factories into a single enterprise so that new ideas reach the assembly line in years rather than decades. Elektrosila, LOMO and Svetlana became models of the approach. Extending it across the Union promises to close the gap between Soviet science and Soviet industry, one of the planned economy's most stubborn weaknesses.
COLDWAR_SOV_gro_the_path: Romanov's Leningrad was known for two things: modern management and an unforgiving hand. As General Secretary, he must choose which of the two will define his rule. He can bet on engineers, computers and automation to make the economy work, or on discipline, ideological vigilance and fear to make people work harder within the existing system.
COLDWAR_SOV_gro_hardline_technocracy: The Soviet Union will be modernised, but strictly on the party's terms. Engineers and economists receive real authority, scientific management and computerised planning spread from the ministries to the shop floor, and productivity becomes the measure of every official. There is no room for liberal experiments or market reforms, for technocracy here means efficiency under firm party control, not freedom.
COLDWAR_SOV_gro_the_intensive_economy: For decades, Soviet growth came from adding more workers, more land and more raw materials, and those reserves are running out. The intensive economy aims to grow instead through productivity, better technology and smarter use of existing capacity, as Leningrad's own experiments suggested. Planners will be judged on efficiency rather than gross output, a quiet revolution in the culture of Gosplan itself.
COLDWAR_SOV_gro_automated_plants: Leningrad's engineers dream of factories run by machines: numerically controlled machine tools, industrial robots and computerised control systems that never drink, never shirk and never miss a shift. Building the microelectronics plants to make this possible is expensive, and Soviet chips still lag behind Western ones, but automation offers a way to raise output without finding workers the country no longer has.
COLDWAR_SOV_gro_iron_discipline: Absenteeism, drinking on the job and falsified reports have become a way of life across the Union. Romanov's answer is discipline: inspections, sanctions, dismissals and the full weight of the KGB behind the party's demands. Republic leaders who inflate their figures will now pay for it, and while the country may grumble, the General Secretary is convinced that order must come before everything else.
COLDWAR_SOV_gro_no_rock_no_jeans: Romanov's Leningrad was notorious for its hostility to the underground rock scene, Western fashion and anything else that smelled of bourgeois decadence. Now the same severity becomes national policy. Unofficial concerts are broken up, black-market jeans are confiscated and youth culture is steered back toward the Komsomol, and while foreign influence weakens, young people and dissidents alike take note.
COLDWAR_SOV_gro_the_purge_of_the_lazy: Too many ministers, directors and obkom secretaries have grown complacent during the long years of stability of cadres. Romanov intends to change that. Officials who miss their targets or live off connections are removed regardless of their patrons and replaced with younger, more demanding managers, and the nomenklatura learns that its positions are no longer guaranteed for life.
COLDWAR_SOV_gro_the_naval_capital: Leningrad has been Russia's naval capital since Peter the Great, and its yards still build the most advanced ships of the Soviet Navy, including the nuclear-powered Kirov-class battlecruisers taking shape at the Baltic Shipyard. Romanov sees the fleet as a symbol of the Union's global reach and pours resources into the shipyards on the Neva, giving Admiral Gorshkov the ocean-going navy he has long demanded.
COLDWAR_SOV_gro_no_concessions: Romanov does not believe in detente. To him, every concession at the negotiating table is a sign of weakness that the imperialists will exploit. Soviet diplomats are instructed to hold firm on every issue, from arms control to human rights, and the military is assured that no agreement will cut its strength. Even fraternal allies hoping for softer trade terms find Moscow unbending.
COLDWAR_SOV_gro_the_baltic_fortress: The Leningrad Military District and the Baltic republics guard the Union's northwestern flank against NATO. Romanov turns the region into a fortress, with new garrisons, fortified coastlines and reinforced border troops. A hard line toward Estonian, Latvian and Lithuanian national sentiment keeps the republics in check ideologically, but deepens a quiet resentment that Moscow would be unwise to ignore.
COLDWAR_SOV_gro_the_heir: Romanov is younger than most of the Politburo, but even a vigorous leader must think about who will follow him. He can gather all power into his own hands and trust that his system will outlive him, or entrust the succession to the defence-industrial technocrats who helped him rise. Either way, the decision will shape the Soviet Union for a generation.
COLDWAR_SOV_gro_the_strong_hand: Romanov has no intention of being merely first among equals. He gathers the levers of power in his own office, overriding the collective leadership that has guided the party since Khrushchev's fall in 1964. Decisions are made faster and enforced more strictly, and those who hesitate are swept aside, for the Soviet Union has its strong hand again, for better or worse.
COLDWAR_SOV_gro_the_technocrats_successi: Romanov chooses institutional continuity over personal rule. Dmitry Ustinov, the veteran master of the defence complex and his closest ally in the Politburo, is designated to take over should the General Secretary die or step down. The arrangement reassures the generals and the industrial ministries that the course of efficiency and military strength will survive any change at the top.
COLDWAR_SOV_gro_the_ordered_union: Under Romanov, the Soviet Union becomes a disciplined and well-managed machine. Plans are fulfilled honestly, factories modernise, scientists and engineers enjoy respect and the authority of the party goes unquestioned. It is a stern and colourless order with little room for dissent or experiment, but for the first time in years the Union seems to be moving with purpose rather than drifting.
COLDWAR_SOV_che_the_apparatchik: Konstantin Chernenko spent his career not on the front lines of politics but behind them, managing paperwork, appointments and correspondence for Leonid Brezhnev. Now the consummate apparatchik leads the party. He offers no grand vision, only the reassurance that the system will go on functioning as it always has, and for a Politburo weary of upheaval that is exactly the point.
COLDWAR_SOV_che_the_general_department: Since 1965, Chernenko has headed the General Department of the Central Committee, the nerve centre through which every Politburo document, decree and secret file must pass. Its archives and procedures are his true power base. By streamlining the department and placing his own people at its desks, he controls what reaches the leadership and when.
COLDWAR_SOV_che_letters_from_the_people: Every year, hundreds of thousands of Soviet citizens write to the Central Committee about housing, shortages, injustice and abuses by local officials. Chernenko's department handles these letters, and he regards them as the ear of the apparatus. Taking the complaints seriously, and acting visibly on a few of them, gives ordinary people the sense that someone in Moscow is listening.
COLDWAR_SOV_che_the_path: Chernenko's instinct is to preserve the system Brezhnev built. Yet the economy is stagnating, the younger members of the Politburo are restless and even loyal apparatchiks admit that something must change. The General Secretary must decide whether to stand firmly on continuity or to permit a careful, limited opening toward the reformers gathered around Gorbachev.
COLDWAR_SOV_che_continuity: There will be no experiments. Cadres stay in their posts, the ministries keep their privileges and the party line remains what it was under Leonid Ilyich. The nomenklatura breathes a sigh of relief and society enjoys a few more years of predictability, while the question of whether the economy can afford this calm is one the old men in the Kremlin prefer not to ask.
COLDWAR_SOV_che_the_ideology_plenum: In June 1983, the Central Committee met in a plenum devoted entirely to ideology, with Chernenko delivering the main report. Its message was clear: Soviet culture, education and propaganda must be purged of foreign influence and rededicated to Marxism-Leninism. Implementing its resolutions tightens the party's hold on the minds of the people, at least on paper.
COLDWAR_SOV_che_a_cautious_opening: Chernenko is no reformer, but he is pragmatic enough to let younger colleagues experiment. Gorbachev and his allies are given room to test new methods in agriculture and industry, provided they do not touch the foundations of the system. It is a small door left ajar, and many in the apparatus fear that it will be impossible to close again.
COLDWAR_SOV_che_the_school_reform: In 1984, the Soviet leadership adopts a sweeping reform of general and vocational schooling. Every pupil is to learn a trade alongside the standard curriculum, and secondary schools are tied more closely to factories and collective farms. The reform promises skilled hands for an economy short of labour, though teachers complain about the added burden and the costs.
COLDWAR_SOV_che_the_food_programme_conti: Brezhnev's Food Programme of May 1982 promised to end the chronic shortages of meat, milk and vegetables by the end of the decade. Chernenko intends to see it through, with more investment in the agro-industrial complex, better storage and transport and higher purchase prices for the collective farms. Grain imports from the capitalist world remain an embarrassment the party hopes to end.
COLDWAR_SOV_che_the_foreign_line: Relations with Washington are at their lowest point in decades. The Euromissile crisis, the downing of KAL 007 and Reagan's talk of an evil empire have poisoned the atmosphere. Chernenko must choose whether to return to the negotiating table in Geneva or to answer American hostility with hostility of his own, beginning with the Olympic Games in Los Angeles.
COLDWAR_SOV_che_the_peace_offensive: The Soviet Union proposes to resume arms talks in Geneva, covering strategic weapons, intermediate-range missiles and weapons in space alike. The offer is aimed at European public opinion as much as at Washington, presenting Moscow as the true champion of peace. Whether the Americans accept, and on what terms, now lies with them.
COLDWAR_SOV_che_the_olympic_boycott: Four years after the Americans boycotted the Moscow Olympics, the Soviet Union answers in kind. Citing security concerns and anti-Soviet hysteria, the National Olympic Committee announces in May 1984 that Soviet athletes will not travel to Los Angeles, and most of the socialist bloc follows. At home the decision is presented as a matter of dignity, while in Washington it confirms that detente is dead.
COLDWAR_SOV_che_the_emphysema: Chernenko is a sick man. Emphysema leaves him breathless, and he spends ever more time at the Kremlin hospital in Kuntsevo while his colleagues govern in his name. The succession can no longer be postponed, and the Politburo must decide whether the next General Secretary will come from the old guard or from a new generation.
COLDWAR_SOV_che_heir_gorbachev: Mikhail Gorbachev already chairs the Secretariat when Chernenko is too ill to attend, and he has quietly built a coalition with Gromyko and the younger members of the Politburo. Naming him heir hands the future to a man of fifty-three who speaks of acceleration and renewal. The old guard is uneasy, but even many of them know the country needs a younger leader.
COLDWAR_SOV_che_heir_grishin: Viktor Grishin has led the Moscow party organisation since 1967 and is the favoured candidate of the Brezhnev-era veterans. A stolid, cautious administrator, he promises that nothing important will change. Elevating him reassures the nomenklatura that its world is safe, though younger cadres and the reformers around Gorbachev see in him only more of the stagnation they despise.
COLDWAR_SOV_che_heir_romanov: Grigory Romanov, the former Leningrad chief who now oversees the defence industry from the Central Committee Secretariat, is the hardliners' answer to Gorbachev. Disciplined, technocratic and uncompromising, he would combine the ideological firmness of the old guard with new managerial energy. Naming him heir signals that the party's future will be one of order rather than reform.
COLDWAR_SOV_che_the_last_of_the_old_guar: Chernenko's rule marks the final chapter of the generation that came of age under Stalin and rose under Brezhnev. They govern with caution, respect for seniority and unshakable faith in the system they built. Their era brings stability and comfort to the apparatus, even as the economy slows and the gap between the leaders and the young grows ever wider.
COLDWAR_SOV_gor_the_new_generation: Mikhail Gorbachev became a full member of the Politburo in October 1980, its youngest by far. Now in power, he represents a generation shaped not by the purges and the war but by the Thaw and the Twentieth Congress. He promises perestroika, a restructuring of the Soviet system, in the belief that socialism can be renewed rather than abandoned.
COLDWAR_SOV_gor_ryzhkov_and_ligachev: Nikolai Ryzhkov, the industrial manager from Sverdlovsk, takes charge of the Council of Ministers, while Yegor Ligachev from Tomsk runs the Secretariat as the party's second man. Together they form the backbone of the new team, one tasked with making the economy work and the other with cleansing the apparatus of corruption and inertia. Their partnership will last only as long as reform stays within limits both can accept.
COLDWAR_SOV_gor_yakovlev_returns: Alexander Yakovlev spent a decade as ambassador in Ottawa, a quiet exile after he criticised Russian nationalism in 1972. Gorbachev met him during his visit to Canada in 1983 and was struck by his ideas. Brought back to Moscow, Yakovlev becomes the intellectual architect of glasnost and the most radical voice in the leadership, convinced that the party must open up in order to survive.
COLDWAR_SOV_gor_shevardnadze_at_the_fore: In July 1985, Andrei Gromyko leaves the Foreign Ministry after twenty-eight years, and Gorbachev hands it to Eduard Shevardnadze, the Georgian party chief with no diplomatic experience at all. The choice stuns the world, but Shevardnadze brings flexibility and warmth where Gromyko was known as Mister Nyet. His appointment also signals respect for the non-Russian republics at the highest level of the Union.
COLDWAR_SOV_gor_the_path: Gorbachev agrees that the system must change, but not on where to begin. Some advisers urge acceleration, modernising machine-building and raising investment so that the economy grows faster before politics is touched. Others argue that nothing will move until the truth can be spoken openly, and that openness must come first, so the order of reform may well decide its fate.
COLDWAR_SOV_gor_uskorenie: At the April Plenum of 1985 and again at the Twenty-Seventh Party Congress, Gorbachev calls for uskorenie, the acceleration of socio-economic development. Massive investment flows into machine-building and new technology, aiming to re-equip Soviet industry within a decade. It is an ambitious but traditional programme of growth from above, and it tests whether the planned economy can still be revived by command.
COLDWAR_SOV_gor_the_anti_alcohol_campaig: In May 1985, the Central Committee declares war on drunkenness. Vodka prices rise, opening hours shrink, vineyards are uprooted and party members are expected to set an example of sobriety. Discipline and public health improve, but the budget loses billions in alcohol revenue, moonshine flourishes and sugar vanishes from the shops, and people soon nickname Gorbachev the mineral water secretary.
COLDWAR_SOV_gor_the_state_enterprise_law: Adopted in June 1987, the Law on the State Enterprise grants factories a measure of self-financing and the right to elect their own directors. State orders replace part of the rigid plan, and enterprises may keep a share of what they earn. The branch ministries lose much of their power in the process, and the planned economy begins to loosen at its very core.
COLDWAR_SOV_gor_glasnost_first: Gorbachev decides that the country cannot be restructured while it is still afraid to speak. Censorship relaxes, papers such as Moscow News and Ogonyok print what was unprintable a year before, and banned films and novels come down from the shelves. Intellectual life flourishes, but the party also loses its monopoly on the truth, and with it a pillar of its authority.
COLDWAR_SOV_gor_the_blank_spots: Soviet history is full of blank spots: the purges, the famine, the secret protocols of 1939, Katyn. Under glasnost, historians and journalists begin to fill them in, Bukharin and other victims of Stalin are rehabilitated and the public learns what the textbooks concealed. The reckoning is cathartic for many, but it shakes the faith of those who believed in the party's infallibility.
COLDWAR_SOV_gor_release_sakharov: Andrei Sakharov, father of the Soviet hydrogen bomb and Nobel Peace laureate, has lived in internal exile in Gorky since 1980. In December 1986, a telephone is suddenly installed in his flat, and the General Secretary himself calls to invite him back to Moscow. His release electrifies the dissident movement and convinces the West that the changes in the Kremlin are real.
COLDWAR_SOV_gor_the_cooperative_law: The Law on Cooperation of May 1988 allows Soviet citizens to found cooperatives in trade, services, catering and even manufacturing. Overnight, much of the shadow economy steps into the light as cafes, repair shops and small producers appear in every city. The state gains taxes and the shops gain goods, though the new cooperators are soon accused of profiteering and ties to organised crime.
COLDWAR_SOV_gor_new_thinking: New political thinking holds that in the nuclear age, universal human values must take precedence over the class struggle. Gorbachev and Shevardnadze apply it to foreign policy, seeking mutual security instead of military superiority. Western leaders are cautiously impressed, and relations with partners across the world begin to thaw as the confrontation of the early 1980s gives way to dialogue.
COLDWAR_SOV_gor_the_zero_option: Reagan proposed the zero option in 1981, expecting Moscow to reject it. Now the Soviet Union takes him at his word: all intermediate-range missiles in Europe, the SS-20 included, are to be eliminated entirely, removing a whole class of nuclear weapons. The generals are furious at giving up more missiles than the Americans, but the decision now rests with Washington.
COLDWAR_SOV_gor_leave_afghanistan: Gorbachev has called Afghanistan a bleeding wound. After years of war, thousands of Soviet dead and no end in sight, the Politburo decides to bring the 40th Army home, offering Kabul a withdrawal plan that gives the Afghan government time to stand on its own. The army sees it as a humiliation, but Soviet mothers will be grateful.
COLDWAR_SOV_gor_the_sinatra_doctrine: The Brezhnev Doctrine is dead. In October 1989, Foreign Ministry spokesman Gennady Gerasimov jokes that Moscow now follows the Sinatra Doctrine, letting the countries of Eastern Europe do it their way, and Soviet tanks will no longer rescue unpopular communist governments. The socialist community saves on subsidies and earns goodwill in the West, but its cohesion can no longer be guaranteed by force.
COLDWAR_SOV_gor_democratisation: At the January Plenum of 1987, Gorbachev declares that perestroika requires the democratisation of party and state. Several candidates are to stand in elections, secret ballots will choose party secretaries and workers may elect their managers. The reformers rejoice, but the nomenklatura sees its appointments and privileges threatened, and the balance of power in the Politburo tips decisively.
COLDWAR_SOV_gor_the_congress_of_peoples_: In March 1989, Soviet citizens vote in the first contested national elections since 1917. The new Congress of People's Deputies brings Sakharov, Yeltsin and many critics of the party onto the national stage, and its sessions, broadcast live, captivate the whole country. Several party bosses lose to unknown challengers, a humiliation that reveals how far the party's authority has fallen.
COLDWAR_SOV_gor_the_union_treaty: The Union of 1922 can no longer hold the republics together by force alone. Gorbachev proposes a new Union Treaty that would turn the Soviet Union into a voluntary federation of sovereign republics, sharing defence, foreign policy and a common market while granting each wide autonomy. A Union-wide referendum is to give it popular legitimacy, but the republics and the hardliners must still be won over.
COLDWAR_SOV_gor_how_far: Perestroika has unleashed forces no one fully controls. Elections, a free press and national movements are reshaping the country faster than the party can adapt. Gorbachev must decide how far the reform should go, whether to keep it within the framework of the Communist Party and its leading role, or to accept that the party itself must become something new.
COLDWAR_SOV_gor_humane_democratic_social: At the Twenty-Eighth Congress in July 1990, the party adopts its programmatic statement Towards a Humane, Democratic Socialism. The Communist Party remains the governing force, but it renounces dogma, accepts political pluralism and commits itself to the rule of law. For Gorbachev, this is the synthesis he has sought since 1985: renewal without rupture, and socialism with a human face at last.
COLDWAR_SOV_gor_the_social_democratic_tu: The reformers conclude that the Communist Party cannot be saved in its old form. Gorbachev and his allies break with the hardliners and refound the governing party on social-democratic principles, modelled on the labour parties of Western Europe, while old comrades denounce the betrayal. The Soviet Union enters uncharted territory as a pluralist socialist state.
COLDWAR_SOV_gor_the_presidency: In March 1990, the Congress of People's Deputies ends the party's constitutional monopoly on power, creates the office of President of the USSR and elects Gorbachev to it. Executive authority shifts from the Politburo to the state. A new Federation Council brings the leaders of all the republics into direct consultation with the President, replacing the old system of party seats.
COLDWAR_SOV_gor_the_common_european_home: In Strasbourg in July 1989, Gorbachev tells the Council of Europe of a common European home stretching from the Atlantic to the Urals. The vision imagines a continent where the blocs dissolve into cooperation, trade flows freely and the Soviet Union takes its place as one European nation among others. The Iron Curtain is lifting, and partners in Bonn, Paris and Rome are eager to engage.
COLDWAR_SOV_wc_all_power_to_the_councils: The slogan of 1917 returns to the streets: all power to the councils. Workers' councils born in factories across the Union demand that the soviets become again what they were meant to be, organs of self-government rather than rubber stamps of the party apparatus. The Free Councils of Labour now hold power, and the ministries, the planners and the nomenklatura brace for a revolution from below.
COLDWAR_SOV_wc_the_novocherkassk_memory: In June 1962, workers at the Novocherkassk electric locomotive plant struck against higher food prices and cut wages. Troops opened fire, killing more than twenty people, and the event was buried in official silence, but Pyotr Siuda, a striker and witness, kept the memory alive. Now Novocherkassk becomes the founding myth of the council movement and a rallying cry for the trade unions.
COLDWAR_SOV_wc_dissolve_the_ministries: The branch ministries in Moscow have commanded Soviet industry from above for half a century. The councils intend to abolish them and hand control of each enterprise to the people who work there. The transition will be chaotic as supply chains break, production falters and old managers resist, but the councils believe that self-management, once rooted, will prove stronger than any bureaucracy.
COLDWAR_SOV_wc_the_council_question: The council revolution must decide where its centre of gravity lies. The industrial workers of the cities, heirs of the Petrograd Soviet, demand that factory councils lead the new order. Yet the countryside has its own claim, for collective farmers want land and autonomy rather than new masters, and the choice between them will shape the character of the new state.
COLDWAR_SOV_wc_factory_councils: Elected councils of workers take over the management of their factories, choosing directors, setting production priorities and sharing the proceeds of their labour. The Yugoslav experience is studied closely, but the Soviet councils aim to go further. Freed from ministerial orders, many enterprises discover unexpected reserves of initiative, and workers see for the first time in decades what it means to own the means of production.
COLDWAR_SOV_wc_the_congress_of_councils: Delegates from councils across the Union gather in Moscow for a Congress of Councils, the first truly elected national assembly of working people since the early days of the revolution. Debates are long, loud and sometimes chaotic, but the Congress gives the new order a face and a voice. Its decrees carry a legitimacy that no Politburo resolution ever enjoyed.
COLDWAR_SOV_wc_the_rural_communes: The collective farms were imposed on the peasantry by force, and those who work them have little say in how they are run. The councils propose a different model: rural communes owned and governed by the people who till the land, free to decide what to grow and how to share the harvest. Productivity rises as farmers at last work for themselves and their neighbours.
COLDWAR_SOV_wc_land_to_the_communes: The land belongs to those who work it. State and collective farms are transferred to the rural communes together with their machinery and livestock, and villages across Russia, Ukraine and Central Asia gain control of their own future. The cities will have to wait longer for consumer goods as resources flow to the countryside, but the peasantry has never been more loyal.
COLDWAR_SOV_wc_the_federation_of_council: The Union of Soviet Socialist Republics was meant to be a free federation of soviet republics, and the councils intend to make that promise real. Power flows upward from local councils to republican congresses and only then to the Union, giving Ukrainians, Georgians, Kazakhs and Balts a genuine voice in their own affairs. Many in the republics find the new federation worth belonging to.
COLDWAR_SOV_wc_abolish_the_nomenklatura: The nomenklatura, the secret lists of posts and of the people entitled to fill them, has been the backbone of party rule since Stalin. The councils abolish it outright: positions are now elected or filled on merit, and special shops, dachas and privileges vanish. Corruption declines sharply, but the displaced elite is bitter and the administrative chaos is felt everywhere.
COLDWAR_SOV_wc_workers_militias: A council republic needs its own defenders. Workers' militias are formed in factories and districts, armed and trained to protect the revolution against counter-revolution and foreign intervention alike. They swell the pool of available manpower, but professional officers watch with alarm as discipline gives way to elected commanders and the regular army loses its monopoly on force.
COLDWAR_SOV_wc_leave_the_arms_race: The councils see the arms race as a burden imposed on working people by two ruling classes. Defence spending is cut sharply, weapons programmes are cancelled and resources are redirected to housing and consumer goods. The generals are outraged, but tensions with the West ease, and workers in Moscow and Detroit alike may wonder why they were ever enemies.
COLDWAR_SOV_wc_international_of_councils: The Soviet council revolution looks abroad for comrades. Yugoslavia, with its long tradition of workers' self-management, becomes the natural first partner, and appeals go out to labour movements from Poland to Latin America. A new international of councils is founded to support self-managing socialism wherever it emerges, offering a third way between Washington and the old Moscow.
COLDWAR_SOV_wc_the_revolutions_course: The councils hold power, but the long-term direction of the revolution remains open. Some delegates insist that it cannot stop at the Soviet borders and must keep advancing at home and abroad. Others argue that the time has come to consolidate, to build stable institutions and to show the world that council communism can work in peace.
COLDWAR_SOV_wc_permanent_revolution: The revolution must never rest. Reviving the old idea of permanent revolution, the councils commit to continuous mobilisation, spreading their model abroad and challenging every entrenched hierarchy at home, while volunteers and aid flow to movements across the world. The energy is intoxicating, but constant upheaval takes its toll on daily life and on stability.
COLDWAR_SOV_wc_the_councils_settle: After years of upheaval, the councils choose consolidation. Procedures are codified, elections become routine and the new institutions settle into the rhythm of everyday government. Workers return to production confident that their councils will endure. The revolution has become a state, and for most citizens that comes as a welcome relief.
COLDWAR_SOV_wc_the_commune_state: The Soviet Union has become what Lenin once described in The State and Revolution: a commune state governed by elected and recallable councils of working people. The ministries and the nomenklatura are gone, factories and farms manage themselves and power flows from below. Utopia or dangerous experiment, the council republic stands as a genuine alternative to capitalism and to the old Soviet model alike.
COLDWAR_SOV_ns_the_iron_line: Sergei Trapeznikov, head of the Central Committee's Department of Science and Education, has long been the voice of those who never accepted the denunciation of Stalin. His Neo-Stalinist Platform now holds power, promising strict discipline, ideological purity and a return to the mobilising spirit of the five-year plans. Intellectuals tremble, but many ordinary people remember the Stalin years as a time of order and greatness.
COLDWAR_SOV_ns_rehabilitate_the_vozhd: Since 1956, Stalin's name has been spoken only in whispers or in condemnation. The Neo-Stalinists restore him as the architect of victory and industrialisation: monuments return, textbooks are rewritten and Khrushchev's secret speech is quietly disowned. In the republics, the memory of the deportations makes the move deeply unpopular, but in Beijing, which never condemned Stalin, Mao takes notice.
COLDWAR_SOV_ns_the_mobilisation_economy: The Neo-Stalinists revive the economics of the 1930s and the war years: maximum investment in heavy and defence industry, rigid central control and the subordination of every resource to the plan. New armaments plants rise and the workforce is placed on a permanent war footing. Living standards suffer and efficiency declines, but the state's capacity to mobilise grows dramatically.
COLDWAR_SOV_ns_the_question: Stalin once declared that cadres decide everything, yet the Neo-Stalinists are also heirs to the five-year plans and the great construction projects. The leadership must choose its emphasis. It can launch a renewed drive of industrialisation powered by ambitious targets, or forge a new and disciplined cadre corps through purges and promotions that will carry the system forward.
COLDWAR_SOV_ns_the_new_industrialisation: Like the first five-year plans, the new industrialisation sets breathtaking targets: new factories, new cities and new industries built at enormous speed. Investment is concentrated on output, and the slogans of the 1930s reappear on factory walls. Civilian industry expands dramatically, but the strain on workers and the disruption of everyday life breed unrest that the regime must contain.
